title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Here's today's research digest across your tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Each section leads with the practical takeaway and the strength of the evidence (RCT vs. review vs. observational), with linked citations below. Informational only — talk to a clinician before acting on anything.

sections.topic: Anti-Aging — Rapamycin, Urolithin A & the NAD Hype
sections.body:
Human longevity data keeps growing, but the honest headline is still **modest effects, no proof of lifespan extension** — so favor interventions with real trials and keep expectations calm.

- **Rapamycin (PEARL trial).** The 48-week, double-blind **PEARL** RCT (healthy adults, weekly placebo vs. 5 mg vs. 10 mg) found low-dose intermittent rapamycin was **relatively safe**, with adverse events similar across groups. Its primary endpoint — **visceral fat — did not change**, but **women on 10 mg** saw significant gains in **lean muscle mass** and less self-reported pain. Efficacy for "longevity" isn't established yet.
- **Urolithin A.** A 2025 *Nature Aging* RCT (50 adults, 1,000 mg/day for 4 weeks) showed UA expanded **younger, less-exhausted CD8+ T cells** and boosted their fat-burning capacity — an encouraging *proof-of-concept* for immune aging, not a longevity outcome.
- **NAD reality check.** A 2026 RCT of an oral NAD+ formula raised **intracellular** blood NAD ~53% but **not** plasma NAD, and **no** clinical, wellbeing, or wearable endpoint held up — a reminder that a moving biomarker isn't a proven benefit.

sections.body:
New 2025–2026 evidence keeps HIIT as a **time-efficient cardio tool** for women — with a clear reminder to **pair it with resistance work and nutrition** for strength and fat loss.

- **Middle-aged & older women.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Physiology* systematic review & meta-analysis (**19 RCTs**, literature through Nov 2025) found HIIT **significantly improved VO2max** (a strong, high-certainty result). Effects on muscle strength were **not** significant, and walking ability improved only borderline — VO2 gains were consistent across ages, body-mass status, and program lengths.
- **Recreationally active women.** A 2025 *Scientific Reports* meta-analysis (15 studies, ~304 women) found **small but real** gains in cardiorespiratory fitness and a **reduction in body-fat percentage**, but **no significant change in total body mass or fat mass**. Expect **recomposition**, not a big shift on the scale.

Bottom line: intensity drives the cardio wins efficiently; **add strength training**, mind nutrition, progress gradually, and keep recovery adequate.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** stays the evidence-based, **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). This week's studies focus on doing it *consistently* and *correctly*.

- **Before surgery, try training first.** A **March 2026** RCT (*Int. Urogynecology Journal*, 90 women awaiting sling surgery) found a supervised **6-week intensive PFMT** program significantly improved **muscle strength** and **symptom severity** vs. education alone — and **43% postponed their planned surgery**. A strong case for structured training before opting for an operation.
- **Adherence is the hard part.** A **Sept 2026** RCT (*BMC Women's Health*) added a self-management ("5E") program to routine care: PFMT **adherence jumped to 74% vs. 32%**, with a bigger drop in weekly leakage episodes.
- **Biofeedback helps postpartum.** A 2024 *JAMA Network Open* RCT (452 new mothers) found adding a **home pressure-biofeedback device** to supervised PFMT more than **doubled the cure rate (20% vs. 9%)**.

Key point: **technique and consistency beat sheer reps** — confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
"Alternative" is best read as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard treatment** — never a replacement for HER2-targeted therapy. Two threads stand out this week.

- **Genomics is refining treatment.** A 2026 *npj Breast Cancer* study (364 HER2+ tumors) found **TP53** mutations were the most common (≈47%) but did **not** predict reduced response to therapy; **PIK3CA** mutations did (pCR 48% vs. 67% with dual HER2 blockade). Useful context: TP53 alone isn't a red flag for HER2 treatment, but tumor genetics increasingly guide care.
- **Vitamin D — being tested properly.** A Phase III RCT (**NCT06642428**, primary completion 2026) is randomizing **vitamin D during neoadjuvant therapy**, measuring pathologic complete response and side effects — a rigorous look at a popular adjunct.
- **Curcumin — temper the hype.** A randomized docetaxel ± **curcumin** trial in advanced breast cancer showed **no improvement** in response or survival (only a small, non-significant PFS trend).

Important: much of this is early or observational. Use integrative options as **add-ons discussed with your oncology team**, and always check for **interactions** with targeted therapy.

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or disjointed sleep, 2026 guidance still puts **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements**.

- **CBT-I is the backbone.** The AASM's 2026 clinical practice guideline on *combination* therapy gives two conditional recommendations: CBT-I **plus** medication beats **medication alone**, but combination is **not** better than **CBT-I alone** — because CBT-I often delivers durable results without drug risks.
- **Restless/disjointed sleep specifically.** In a randomized study of people with **restless legs syndrome plus insomnia**, just **4 sessions of CBT-I** improved insomnia severity, **sleep efficiency, total sleep time, time to fall asleep, and night-time awakenings**, plus anxiety — with benefits lasting **3 months**. (Small, older 2020 trial, but directly on-topic.) If sleep is fragmented, ask a provider to rule out **restless legs** and **sleep apnea**.
- **Melatonin, honestly.** The AASM suggests melatonin is best for **circadian timing** problems (jet lag, shift work), **not** chronic insomnia.

Best habits: keep a **fixed wake time**, reserve the bed for sleep, keep the room cool/dark/quiet, and dim screens during wind-down.
